title: No one has ever caught an adult bigfin squid: it is known only from cameras

cover.alt: A pale, translucent squid with two large, rounded fins hovers in dark blue water, its long thin arms spreading out below it.

body: Bigfin squid live in the deep ocean around the world, yet sightings are rare and **no adult has ever been collected**; only juveniles have been caught. Almost everything known about the adults comes from cameras on submarines. Their arms and tentacles look identical: they stick out sideways, then bend down sharply, like elbows, and trail far below. Scientists suspect they feed by dragging those arms along the seafloor, or simply wait for prey to bump into them.

slides.alt: A bigfin squid hangs in the dark water, flapping two large, rounded fins, while its many long, white arms bend outwards and trail down out of the frame.
slides.caption: Filmed by a NOAA robot submarine 2,385 m down in the Gulf of Mexico in 2021: a bigfin squid flaps its large fins, its long arms bending sharply at their ‘elbows’.
slides.credit: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Windows to the Deep 2021 · Public domain · excerpt

slides.label: estimated length of the largest bigfin squid, mostly arms
slides.text: Some estimates go as high as 12 m. They all come from video, because no adult has ever been measured in the hand.

slides.prompt: When was an adult bigfin squid first caught on camera?
slides.detail: Since then it has turned up in footage from deep-sea expeditions all over the world, but always as a rare encounter.

slides.question: What gives the bigfin squid's arms their ‘elbows’?
options: They stick out sideways, then bend down
Joints with tiny bones in them
They fold in half to swim
slides.explanation: Squid have no bones. The arms and tentacles are held out at right angles to the body before turning down, which looks like a bend at the elbow.
